The constraints that come from the deployment target rather than the mathematics. Ethereum wants blocks proved in seconds, on modest hardware, at a security level nobody is willing to negotiate — and increasingly with post-quantum assumptions. See protocol snarkification for the broader effort, and Safely Snarkifying the Ethereum Protocol for the talk.

That framing is what the August 2026 decision to drop Poseidon for L1 inverts, and this page should be written with the reversal in view: hash-friendly SNARKs rather than SNARK-friendly hashes. The cost question below is still the right question — the answer simply stopped selecting for an exotic primitive.

Ethereum's workhorse is keccak256, and it is not SHA-3. Keccak won the NIST competition in 2012, NIST changed the padding rule before standardising it as FIPS 202 in 2015, and Ethereum had already shipped the original. The two differ in padding and produce different digests for the same input, which is a reliable source of confusion for anyone reimplementing an Ethereum client.

It is used almost everywhere state is named. An address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak digest of a public key; a mapping's storage slot is the digest of the key concatenated with the slot number; Merkle–Patricia trie nodes are addressed by the digest of their RLP encoding; function selectors and event topics are digest prefixes; and the KECCAK256 opcode exposes it to contracts directly.

The consensus layer chose differently. SSZ's hash_tree_root is SHA-256, so a full node computes both families — Keccak for execution state and SHA-256 for beacon state. The EVM also exposes SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 as precompiles at 0x02 and 0x03, and BLAKE2b's compression function at 0x09 (EIP-152, Istanbul, December 2019, priced at one gas per round).

For a prover this split matters, because the execution state is the Keccak half. Keccak is the most expensive of the three to prove — Flock reports 30k Keccak permutations per second per core against 42k SHA-256 compressions — though the gap per byte is narrower than the raw rates suggest, since one Keccak-256 permutation absorbs 136 bytes where a SHA-256 compression takes 64.
A map of the layers, so that a claim about one system can be compared with a claim about another. Worth writing before the pages below it.
